.@LassieAI co-founder and CEO Steijn Pelle says small businesses like doctors' offices should run themselves:

"The busy work is done by agents."

"We want to build agents for the business that then will interface with the personal agent of a consumer."

"It needs to really work, and the onboarding needs to be as simple as onboarding on Coinbase or Stripe."

"All small businesses at an abstract level have a system of record they need to read and write into. They all have customers... it's interacting and transacting around payments. You need to book appointments."

"The end goal is if we served all the doctor offices, that we help all the small businesses across the world."

@steijnpelle

tweets.text:
The Situational Awareness situation.

It is now being reported that the AI hedge fund has exited its entire public equity portfolio this month.

But, what does this really mean?

As of July 1st, the Net Asset Value (NAV) of the fund is now being reported to have been ~$45 billion.

First, let's put this into perspective.

NAV = (Assets − Liabilities). This is the fund's equity capital, also known as the investors' money after accounting for borrowings.

This is NOT the same as the size of the fund's positions, particularly because the fund has been known for utilizing extreme amounts of leverage. For example:

1. At 2x leverage, a $45 billion NAV supports ~$90 billion of gross market exposure
2. At 3x leverage, that rises to ~$135 billion

The same insurer pays up to 2.09x as much for identical service depending on the state.

28% of claims get approved and then sent back over a code, a form, a missing field.

My thoughts on the Fed that told us nothing and how the bond market responded. 

Rates unchanged yesterday, exactly as I told you. 

That was the easy part. What came with it was nothing. No forward guidance, not one sentence about September. The statement barely moved except for the dissent list.

3 dissents. Logan, Hammack, Kashkari, all for 25 bps. FinX called it a hawkish tell. It isn’t. Warsh wants the argument in the open, where prior chairs got unanimity that was mostly theater. So 3 dissents under him means less, not more, and those 3 have been the hawkish end of the table all along.

The market moved my way. September hike odds fell to 60% from 80%. Fewer people believe a hike is coming, not more, and that number still has room to fall.

Now the part everyone should be focusing on.

The most important market yesterday was Treasuries. The 30-year rose 12.1 bps to 5.213%, highest since 2007. Real yields rose with it, so the actual cost of capital got worse. 10s2s steepened. That is a bond market pricing a Fed behind the curve, and pricing it aggressively.

The fear is not really about oil. What’s spooking the long end is AI capex. Chips and memory. Power. Copper, silver and gold all higher the same day. One commodity rising is a story about that commodity. All of them rising at once is capital being fire hosed into every physical corner of the economy.

I’ll say the thing I always say, because I believe it and because it limits how far I’ll push this. Sustained inflation is a monetary phenomenon. Oil doubling is a relative price change. But when hundreds of billions chase a fixed stock of transformers, turbines, HBM capacity and electricians on four-year lead times, the money is real and the supply is finite, and the bond market has decided that’s close enough. Whether it’s textbook correct matters less than the 30-year sitting at 5.21% and still climbing.

Which gives you the ugliest setup I’ve seen in a while, because stocks and bonds want opposite things.

Stocks want a cut, or a clear one-and-done hike so the pain has an end date. Bonds want a hike badly, because that’s the only way this Fed shows resolve on inflation. Bonds aren’t asking nicely. They’re selling until they get an answer.

The best outcome for both is the Fed telegraphing 25 bps for September. Calms the long end, doesn’t signal a cycle. I don’t think they deliver it, same as I didn’t think they’d hike.

Until they do, you’re long a tape where the bond market votes against you every day.

I think that communicating a reaction function is a clear positive for market stability. Even a rote Taylor Rule would suffice.

If the Fed were a single-mandate central bank (i.e. only price stability represented by an inflation goal), then this would not be a big deal.

However, the dual mandate requires explanation of how the CB synthesizes/interprets incoming data and balances the competing mandates (inflation vs employment). This communication is especially important when the typical Philip's Curve framework breaks down (i.e. inflation is coming from supply/investment cycles not a tight jobs market).
